title: Beyond minimizers: stationary harmonic maps and computable regularity constants
summary: From Evans's sphere theorem to general targets: the Rivière–Struwe proof in Lean, and exact rational bounds for the small-energy threshold and Hölder estimate.
text: After formalizing small-energy regularity for energy-minimizing harmonic maps, the next question is natural: how much of the conclusion survives if we retain the first variations but give up the minimizing inequality? This leads to stationary harmonic maps, where the geometry still produces a monotonicity formula, but the comparison argument from the minimizing case is no longer available. The previous post followed a proof built around harmonic replacement, projection, and admissible competitors. The stationary project instead uses an antisymmetric system, a Coulomb frame, and compensated estimates. It also makes the small-energy threshold and the Hölder coefficient computable from certified geometric data. The mathematical story has three parts: how small-energy regularity passed from spheres to general targets, which proof route the formalization follows, and how the constants in that route become exact rational numbers. The result, at a glance For every source dimension n ≥ 2 , a stationary weakly harmonic map into a compact embedded C 2 target has a unique C 0 , 1 / 2 representative on the inner half ball when its normalized energy is sufficiently small. For a smooth target, the same representative is smooth. Given a certified extension of the normal projection and a rational derivative bound, the energy threshold and Hölder coefficient are explicit rational-valued functions. Their values are conservative admissible bounds. From minimizing maps to stationary maps Let N ⊂ R q be a nonempty compact embedded submanifold without boundary, and let Ω ⊂ R n be open. We keep the energy convention of the minimizing project: E ( u ; B ) = ∫ B ∣ D u ∣ H S 2 d x , Θ u ( a , r ) = r 2 − n E ( u ; B r ( a ) ) . There is no factor of one half. The displayed weak gradient D u is the same object in Sobolev membership, the variational identities, and the energy. Weak harmonicity is the vanishing of the first variation under compactly supported tangent variations of the map. Domain stationarity is a further identity: for every X ∈ C c ∞ ( Ω , R n ) , ∫ Ω ∣ D u ∣ 2 div ⁡ X d x = 2 ∫ Ω ∑ i , j = 1 n ⟨ D i u , D j u ⟩ ∂ i X j d x . In this post, a stationary harmonic map satisfies both conditions. An energy minimizer supplies them, but neither first-variation identity supplies the inequality against arbitrary competitors that a minimizing proof uses. At weak regularity, domain stationarity must also be stated explicitly; it is not silently inferred from weak harmonicity. The distinction changes the proof. Monotonicity survives because its input is the domain-stationarity identity. The energy comparison with a projected harmonic replacement requires minimality. To recover decay for stationary maps, the argument must use more of the structure of the weak equation. How the theory reached general targets The classical background begins with Schoen and Uhlenbeck's 1982 regularity theory for energy-minimizing harmonic maps . Passing to stationary maps required a different argument, since their energy need not decrease under finite variations. A key special case was the sphere. In 1991, Lawrence C. Evans proved partial regularity for stationary harmonic maps into spheres. His proof combined the sphere's algebraic structure with compensated estimates and Hardy–BMO duality. The exceptional set has zero ( n − 2 ) -dimensional Hausdorff measure. In 1993, Fabrice Béthuel extended this stationary regularity theory to general compact Riemannian targets. Thus the general-target theorem predates the later antisymmetric-system formulation. The issue for formalization is which proof of that theorem to implement. Work Setting Place in the argument Schoen–Uhlenbeck, 1982 Energy-minimizing maps The minimizing regularity theory underlying the previous project Evans, 1991 Stationary maps into spheres Uses the sphere's special structure and compensation Béthuel, 1993 Stationary maps into general compact targets Extends the stationary theory beyond spheres Rivière–Struwe, 2008 Antisymmetric systems with critical Morrey control Supplies the gauge method chosen for this formalization Tristan Rivière's antisymmetric formulation reorganized two-dimensional conformally invariant variational equations. Rivière and Michael Struwe then developed the higher-dimensional method in Partial regularity for harmonic maps and related problems , published in 2008. Its Theorem 2.1 treats the stationary small-energy problem for closed C 2 targets in dimensions at least three. The preprint appeared in 2006. Their method combines a skew-symmetric coefficient, a Coulomb gauge, and critical Morrey estimates. It avoids constructing a frame adapted to the target's tangent bundle and makes the C 2 geometric assumption explicit. The present project follows this route, including dimension two in its public theorem. The theorem selected for Lean Fix n ≥ 2 and a compact embedded C 2 target N ⊂ R q , with its induced Euclidean metric. Suppose u ∈ W l o c 1 , 2 ( Ω , R q ) , u ( x ) ∈ N for almost every x , and suppose u is weakly harmonic under tangent map variations and domain stationary. The formal theorem supplies ε ∗ > 0 and C ≥ 0 , depending only on n , N , with the following conclusion. If B R ( a ) ‾ ⊂ Ω , Θ u ( a , R ) ≤ ε ∗ , then there is a unique continuous representative w on B R / 2 ( a ) . It agrees with u almost everywhere, takes values in N at every point, and satisfies ∣ w ( x ) − w ( y ) ∣ ≤ C R − 1 / 2 Θ u ( a , R ) ∣ x − y ∣ 1 / 2 , x , y ∈ B R / 2 ( a ) . The exponent is fixed at α = 1 / 2 . The constants are chosen before the domain, map, weak gradient, center, and radius. The statement includes zero energy and covers the entire inner half ball. Uniqueness is among all continuous ambient-valued representatives agreeing almost everywhere with u there. For a compact smooth target, a second theorem proves that this same w is C ∞ , retaining the quantitative Hölder bound. Its public statement does not include quantitative estimates for every derivative order. The C 2 theorem and the smooth-target corollary therefore have distinct conclusions. The proof route: geometry, gauge, compensation Let Q ( y ) be the orthogonal projection onto the normal space ( T y N ) ⊥ . The embedded C 2 geometry makes Q a C 1 field along N . Choose a compactly supported ambient C 1 extension G and a bound ℓ for its derivative. Tangency of the weak gradient and the original tangent variations give an antisymmetric equation: − Δ u = ∑ i = 1 n A i D i u , where A i = Q ( u ) ∂ i ( Q ∘ u ) − ∂ i ( Q ∘ u ) Q ( u ) , A i T = − A i . This commutator also gives ∣ A ∣ H S ≤ 2 q ℓ ∣ D u ∣ H S . The skew symmetry is the structure that the compensation argument exploits. An arbitrary quadratic right-hand side would not carry this information. Independently, domain stationarity gives the exact monotonicity identity: Θ u ( a , s ) − Θ u ( a , r ) = 2 ∫ B s ( a ) ∖ B r ( a ) ∣ x − a ∣ 2 − n ∣ ∂ r a d , a u ∣ 2 d x ≥ 0. Monotonicity at nearby centers converts small energy on the original ball into control on all smaller balls. To state that control precisely, write M 2 ( F ; D ) 2 = sup ⁡ x ∈ D t > 0 t 2 − n ∫ B t ( x ) ∩ D ∣ F ∣ 2 d x . For D = B 3 R / 4 ( a ) , the proof obtains M 2 ( D u ; D ) 2 + M 2 ( A ; D ) 2 ≤ M Θ u ( a , R ) , with the explicit geometric factor M = ( 1 + 4 q ℓ 2 ) 4 n − 2 . This is the link between stationarity and the gauge construction. A single integral on one ball becomes critical Morrey control of both the original gradient and its connection. For sufficiently small connection, the proof constructs P ∈ W 1 , 2 ( D , S O ( q ) ) such that Z i = P T ∂ i P + P T A i P is divergence-free with its natural zero normal flux. Its Morrey bound controls D P and this actual transformed connection together. No orientation of N or global normal frame is required, and the main theorem does not ask the caller to supply a gauge. From stationarity to one regular representative Domain stationarity gives exact monotonicity and all-center critical Morrey control. Compact target geometry and tangent weak harmonicity give the signed normal-projection antisymmetric system. These inputs construct a critical Coulomb frame, compensated Hodge estimates and envelope contraction, yielding a unique target-valued Hölder representative on the entire half ball. A smooth target permits a Poisson bootstrap of this same representative to smoothness. 01 / REGULARITY From stationarity to regularity n ≥ 2 · compact embedded target · small normalized energy Domain stationarity Stress identity · radial tests Compact C 2 target Tangent weak harmonicity Exact monotonicity Θ u ( a , r ) ≥ Θ u ( a , s ) ( s ≤ r ) Normal-projection commutator A i = [ G ( u ) , ∂ i ( G ∘ u ) ] Critical Morrey control Centers in B 3 R / 4 ( a ) · every radius Signed antisymmetric system − Δ u = ∑ i A i D i u Critical Coulomb frame P ∈ S O ( q ) · natural boundary identity Compensated Hodge estimates One cutoff · one decomposition Envelope contraction ∫ B r ( x ) ∣ D v ∣ p ≤ C η p r n − p / 2 Unique target-valued representative w ∈ C 0 , 1 / 2 ( B R / 2 ( a ) , N ) Smooth target Same-map Poisson bootstrap Preserve the original weak gradient The same w is smooth On the entire open half ball Mathematical dependencies, not an import graph Figure 1. Stationarity and weak harmonicity supply different inputs. Morrey control makes the connection small enough for the frame construction; the signed equation enters the compensated estimates. The smooth-target upgrade also uses the weak equation and target geometry. Arrows summarize mathematical dependencies. The next step applies a Hodge decomposition to a genuine cutoff v of the original map minus its mean. The exact part, coexact part, and harmonic remainder are retained through their estimates. Div–curl compensation controls the difficult pairings, and an all-center envelope iteration yields improved gradient growth. With p = 1 + 1 / ( 2 n ) , its bound has the form ∫ B r ( x ) ∣ D v ∣ p d x ≤ C p o w η p r n − p / 2 , where η controls the joint Morrey amplitude. This is an L p growth estimate for the cutoff, from which the Morrey argument recovers exponent 1 / 2 for the original map. Compactness of the actual target supplies the bounded cutoff needed in these pairings. Accordingly, the project proves the compact-target harmonic-map theorem; it does not export a general regularity theorem for arbitrary, possibly unbounded Euclidean-valued antisymmetric systems. Ball averages then recover the continuous representative, its almost-everywhere agreement with u , its pointwise target values, and its uniqueness. Applying the intermediate two-thirds-ball estimate on B 3 R / 4 ( a ) reaches exactly B R / 2 ( a ) . For a smooth target, the same representative satisfies a quadratic Poisson equation with smooth geometric coefficients. The reused analytic infrastructure proves a classical first derivative and then applies Poisson Schauder estimates and a smooth bootstrap. This is where the stationary development reconnects with the earlier minimizing project. What the geometric certificate contains An abstract existence theorem says that its constants depend only on n , N . Numerical evaluation needs a finite geometric input. Here that input is a certified pair ( G , ℓ ) : G ∈ C c 1 ( R q , L ( R q , R q ) ) , ℓ ∈ Q ≥ 0 , G ( y ) = Q ( y ) ( y ∈ N ) , ∥ D G ( y ) ∥ o p ≤ ℓ ( y ∈ R q ) . The derivative bound must hold throughout the ambient extension, including its cutoff region. A bound only along N does not supply this certificate. The norm convention matters: D G maps Euclidean vectors to matrices equipped with their operator norm. Gradient and connection energies use the Hilbert–Schmidt norm. The factor 4 q ℓ 2 above records the corresponding estimate. The formal development proves that every target in the theorem admits suitable data. It also proves an effective theorem when those data are supplied. It does not assert an algorithm extracting a numerical certificate from an arbitrary abstract manifold. Once the certificate is available, evaluating the constants requires no computation of the map or its Coulomb frame. Closing the constant calculation The effective interface uses four positive rational coefficients depending only on n , q : Coefficient Role κ Smallness threshold for constructing the critical Coulomb frame C g Joint Morrey bound for the frame gradient and transformed connection θ Smallness threshold for the compensated argument with a given frame C r Hölder coefficient from that argument and representative construction With these coefficients, the final calculation is M = ( 1 + 4 q ℓ 2 ) 4 n − 2 , K = ( 1 + C g ) ( 1 + M ) , ε ∗ = ( min ⁡ { κ , θ } K ) 2 , C = 2 C r K , α = 1 2 . The energy threshold enforces both smallness conditions. The coefficient K absorbs the geometric and frame estimates; the final factor 2 accounts for transporting the intermediate representative estimate to the required half ball. The calculation continues below this final formula. The constant ledger expands the Sobolev, Hardy, projection, boundary, moment, and iteration coefficients. Even the cutoff is quantified: ∣ D χ ∣ ≤ 2 24 , ∣ Δ χ ∣ ≤ 2 48 + 2 25 n , with χ = 1 on B 2 / 3 and χ = 0 outside B 3 / 4 at unit scale. For the decay iteration, the ledger chooses rational scales. If D 0 denotes its one-step coefficient and H = 512 D 0 , then ϑ = ( 2 + 8 H ) − 2 , θ = ϑ n 4 ( 1 + H ) , σ = ϑ 16 . Here ϑ is a spatial contraction scale; θ is a smallness threshold. Their distinct roles are preserved in the calculation. Nonrational intermediate expressions are replaced by proved rational majorants. For x ≥ 0 , for example, x 1 / p ≤ 1 + x ( p ≥ 1 ) , x p ≤ ( 1 + x ) 2 ( 1 ≤ p ≤ 2 ) . The resulting public functions, effectiveStationaryEnergyThreshold and effectiveStationaryHolderConstant , use integer and rational arithmetic. The paper includes a self-contained evaluator for the complete definitions. This gives a stronger numerical interface than the constant extraction discussed in the previous post: the effective theorem itself uses the explicit rational-valued functions. Positivity and admissibility are proved for those functions, and the original existential target-only theorem remains available. What the numbers actually are The repository evaluates the arithmetic at n = 2 , q = 3 , ℓ = 1. For these inputs, M = 13 , K = 14 ( 1 + C g ) , and the gauge coefficient is the exact rational C g = 175029176740443082956099856 67453 . The intermediate values locate the losses: Coefficient Approximate value κ 5.708774008778 × 10 − 277 C g 2.594831612240 × 10 21 θ 5.422403690448 × 10 − 3192 C r 4.062194913898 × 10 5749 In this example θ < κ . The given-frame compensated iteration therefore imposes the smaller of the two thresholds. Substituting into the final formula gives ε ∗ ≈ 2.227969608538 × 10 − 6428 , C ≈ 2.951399297746 × 10 5772 . Equivalently, log ⁡ 10 ε ∗ ≈ − 6427.652090738 , log ⁡ 10 C ≈ 5772.470027970. The exact value of ε ∗ has numerator 4549907209 and a denominator with 6,438 decimal digits. The exact value of C has a 5,778-digit numerator and denominator 67453 . The downloadable rational data preserve all those digits. The displayed decimals are rounded evaluations. Integer cross multiplication verifies the coarser bounds 10 − 6428 ≤ ε ∗ < 10 − 6427 , 10 5772 ≤ C < 10 5773 . The repository's numerical checker was rerun for this post. It evaluated the public Lean functions and matched every numerator and denominator against the committed data. These values quantify an admissible proof, not an optimal regularity threshold. Large majorants accumulate through boundary estimates, gauge construction, compensation, and iteration. Also, ( 2 , 3 , 1 ) is an arithmetic input example: it does not certify ℓ = 1 for the unit sphere or any particular target embedding. Applying these numbers to a target requires the geometric certificate described above. Code and mathematical sources This account uses the 27 October 2026 repository revision . The public entry points are: module public import StationaryHarmonicMaps #check StationaryHarmonicMaps.stationary_small_energy_regularity #check StationaryHarmonicMaps.stationary_small_energy_smooth_regularity #check StationaryHarmonicMaps.stationary_small_energy_regularity_effective #check StationaryHarmonicMaps.stationary_small_energy_smooth_regularity_effective The repository contains the stationary library and the reused Sobolev and smooth-bootstrap libraries. Its verification guide documents source, complete-statement, axiom-closure, consumer, numerical, and kernel-replay checks. The allowed theorem-closure axioms are propext , Classical.choice , and Quot.sound . The fresh project check reported here is the exact-constant reproduction; preparing this post did not rerun the full Lean build or kernel replay. title: From small energy to singular sets: formalizing harmonic maps in Lean
summary: How a classical regularity proof becomes a reusable formal interface—and how that interface supports compactness, tangent maps, and singular-set stratification.
text: “Compare with a suitable competitor.” In an analysis proof, that phrase can fit on one line. In Lean, it opens a substantial list of obligations: construct the map, identify its weak derivatives, match its traces, preserve its target constraint, and prove that it belongs to the comparison class. Those obligations shaped my formalization of two classical results for energy-minimizing harmonic maps: small-energy regularity and singular-set stratification. The second development imports the first. Together, they connect a local estimate on a ball with a geometric description of where smoothness can fail. This post follows that connection. The central question is how to organize a proof so that its mathematical choices remain visible while an AI coding agent handles much of the formal implementation. The most useful decisions concerned the proof route, the objects shared between lemmas, and the induction needed to work in every dimension. The two results, at a glance Small energy: one smooth representative, with a single threshold that works for every derivative order. Singular sets: that regularity theorem becomes an input to compactness, tangent maps, and classical Hausdorff-dimension bounds. The bridge is built from mathematical interfaces: the same map, the same connector, and precisely the assumptions the next argument needs. What small energy actually gives Fix n ≥ 2 and a nonempty compact smooth embedded submanifold N ⊂ R q , without boundary, with its induced metric. Let Ω ⊂ R n be open. Here a minimizing map is an N -valued u ∈ W l o c 1 , 2 ( Ω , R q ) that minimizes energy on every ball compactly contained in Ω , against N -valued Sobolev competitors whose difference from u lies in W 0 1 , 2 on that ball. The normalization is Θ u ( a , r ) = r 2 − n ∫ B r ( a ) ∣ D u ∣ H S 2 d x . There is no factor of one half. Scaling is built into this quantity: it measures the energy relevant to regularity at the scale of the ball. For each n , N , the formalized theorem supplies ε ∗ > 0 , 0 < γ < 1 , and finite nonnegative constants C k . If B R ( a ) ‾ ⊂ Ω and Θ u ( a , R ) ≤ ε ∗ , then u has a unique continuous representative w on B R / 2 ( a ) . This representative is smooth, takes values in N , and satisfies sup ⁡ B R / 2 ( a ) ∣ w − w ( a ) ∣ ≤ C 0 Θ u ( a , R ) . For every k ≥ 1 , it also satisfies R k sup ⁡ B R / 2 ( a ) ∥ D k w ∥ ≤ C k Θ u ( a , R ) and R k + γ [ D k w ] γ ; B R / 2 ( a ) ≤ C k Θ u ( a , R ) . The order of these choices matters. The threshold, exponent, and entire sequence of constants are chosen before the domain, map, displayed weak gradient, ball, and derivative order. Every estimate concerns the same representative . The threshold does not become smaller each time another derivative is requested. The precise endpoint is HolderToCK.smallEnergySmoothRegularity . It includes dimension two and zero energy. Its uniqueness assertion is local to the half ball; it does not prescribe an ambient extension outside it. Choosing the proof before generating code Classical regularity theory offers several routes to this conclusion. A compactness argument can be short on paper, but its formal dependencies may include a substantial interpolation theorem. A more direct comparison argument can expose its scales and smallness conditions, while demanding detailed work on smoothing and admissibility. I followed the Schoen–Uhlenbeck route presented in Section 10.3.1 of Giaquinta–Martinazzi : uniform smoothing, harmonic replacement, tubular projection, and energy comparison. This made it possible to obtain regularity before constructing the full Luckhaus interpolation machinery needed later for compactness. The sequence is concrete. Minimality gives stationarity and monotonicity. Smoothing produces a smooth ambient map near N . Harmonic replacement improves the interior energy. Projection returns the replacement to the target, and variable smoothing joins it to the original map across a shell. Only after the boundary and Sobolev obligations are proved can minimality be applied. The result is one-step energy decay. Rescaling and iteration produce decay at smaller scales, and a Morrey estimate yields a Hölder representative. In the variable-smoothing calculation, even the full derivative matrix and Jacobian must survive the translation into Lean. These details determine whether the competitor is admissible. This is a choice of dependency order. Harmonic replacement remains part of the argument, compactness of the target still supplies geometric bounds, and some constants are selected existentially. The chosen route gives a chain of estimates that can be inspected and reused. From small energy to one smooth representative A mathematical dependency diagram for interior regularity of energy-minimizing harmonic maps. Target geometry and stationarity lead to one-step energy decay, then a Hölder representative. The weak equation also enters the same-map C1 gamma estimate. A separate Poisson Schauder estimate feeds the higher-order bootstrap. The conclusion uses one energy threshold and the same representative at every derivative order. 01 / REGULARITY One threshold. One representative. n ≥ 2 · smooth compact target · interior minimizing maps Target geometry Projection · weak Euler equation Stationarity & monotonicity Control of scaled energy One-step energy decay Θ u ( 0 , τ ) ≤ 1 2 E ( u ; B 1 ) Hölder representative Iteration · Morrey estimate · map w Same-map C 1 , γ estimate Identify the classical and weak gradients Weak equation Poisson Schauder estimate Higher-order bootstrap Differentiate · estimate · iterate Unique smooth representative w One ε ∗ · one sequence C k · every derivative order Shared analytic input Mathematical dependencies, not an import graph Figure 1. The regularity proof separates the construction of a Hölder representative from its analytic upgrade. Geometry and the weak equation also enter the upgrade; the Schauder estimate is an independent input to higher derivatives. The arrows summarize mathematical dependencies, not every source-file import. From a Hölder map to a smooth map The second part of regularity begins with a map that is continuous but still has only a weak gradient. A smooth coefficient A obtained from the target geometry gives a quadratic Poisson equation: Δ w = F , F = ∑ i = 1 n A ( w ) [ D i w , D i w ] . The upgrade library first treats this as a general analytic problem. Its interfaces retain the actual map, its displayed weak gradient, and the signed weak equation. Harmonic maps are then an application of that analysis. The first derivative is the difficult bridge. Comparison with a harmonic replacement gives improved energy growth and gradient-excess decay. A Campanato argument produces a Hölder representative of the weak gradient; mollification then identifies it as the classical derivative of the same w . The exponent at this step is γ = α / 8 , where α is the initial Hölder exponent. Once this bridge is established, a weak Poisson Schauder estimate and differentiated equations support the higher-order induction. The Schauder proof includes the point contribution in the distributional Hessian of the fundamental solution. Omitting that term would change the equation being proved. Separating the two parts has a useful mathematical consequence: one can use the Hölder theorem without importing the entire higher-order analysis, and the quadratic-Poisson theorem can be applied to coefficients that do not come from harmonic maps. Connecting the parts requires the continuous and smooth representatives to agree almost everywhere and hence, by continuity, throughout their common domain. The same witness must survive every step A recurring challenge is easy to express logically. A theorem that supplies one map with a good energy bound and another map close to the target does not supply a map with both properties. Yet a geometric comparison may require precisely that conjunction. This becomes central in Luckhaus interpolation. Two Sobolev maps on a sphere are joined by one ambient-valued connector on a thin cylinder, with thickness 0 < ϵ < 1 / 8 . The connector must simultaneously have the prescribed endpoint traces, an energy bound, and a distance-to-target bound. The distance estimate permits projection into a tubular neighborhood; the energy estimate controls the resulting competitor. The connector is not required to take values in N before projection. It also carries compatible weak-gradient data and an annular extension. These are properties of the same construction, rather than independent existential outputs. The thickness restriction has mathematical content. Extending the stated distance estimate to arbitrary large thicknesses would be false even for a compact target consisting of two points. Formalization therefore makes it important to preserve the version needed by the proof, including its quantifiers and geometric restrictions. Mathematical targets, shared witnesses and two forms of verification The regularity argument retains one representative across all derivative orders; the Luckhaus construction retains one connector whose traces, energy and distance estimates hold together. Formal proofs need both statement review, which checks that the type expresses the intended mathematics, and proof checking under declared axioms. These are separate obligations. 02 / THE PROOF CONTRACT Keep the conclusions attached to one witness. The object being constructed is part of the mathematical interface. Mathematical target Shared witness Joint conclusions REGULARITY Small scaled energy An interior ball A minimizing Sobolev map One representative w Agrees with u a.e. Same map, every order Smoothness & bounds One threshold ε ∗ All derivative orders LUCKHAUS INTERPOLATION Two Sobolev traces Thin-cylinder data 0 < ϵ < 1 / 8 One connector w Shared gluing data Coherent weak gradients Joint guarantees Traces + energy control Distance-to-target control Two checks, two questions Statement review Does the type express the intended mathematical statement? Proof checking Does the proof justify that type under the declared axioms? Semantic fidelity and proof-term validity are separate obligations. Figure 2. A useful interface preserves a common witness across all conclusions. For the Luckhaus construction, traces, weak gradients, energy and distance estimates must describe one connector. For regularity, the continuity and derivative estimates must describe one representative. From regularity to the shape of singularities The stratification project imports the regularity library at a fixed revision. It shares its Sobolev spaces, energy normalization, target geometry, and comparison class. Small-energy regularity enters as a proved theorem. Luckhaus interpolation supplies admissible competitors for the compactness argument. The proof establishes that a weak limit remains minimizing and that local energies converge. Combined with weak convergence of the gradients, convergence of their squared Hilbert norms gives strong local convergence. Limit minimality and energy convergence are conclusions of this argument, not extra assumptions. Strong compactness then produces tangent maps along subsequences of any prescribed sequence of shrinking positive scales. Monotonicity shows that these limits are homogeneous. The tangent relation is defined by actual strong local map-and-gradient convergence; target values, minimality, homogeneity, and the energy identity are subsequently proved for its limits. Let Σ ( u ) denote the interior singular set, and let Θ u ( a ) be the limiting density as the radius tends to zero. For a homogeneous tangent φ , its spine S ( φ ) is the linear subspace characterized by S ( φ ) = { z : Θ φ ( z ) = Θ φ ( 0 ) } . Translation along this subspace leaves the tangent map unchanged almost everywhere. The j -th stratum consists of points in Σ ( u ) at which every actual tangent map has spine dimension at most j . Tangent maps need not be unique. Under the same minimizing-map assumptions, for n ≥ 3 and 0 ≤ j ≤ n − 3 , the formalized result gives dim ⁡ H S j ( u ) ≤ j , H s ( S j ( u ) ) = 0 for every s > j . The top three strata agree with the singular set, so dim ⁡ H Σ ( u ) ≤ n − 3 . In dimension three there is no accumulation of singular points anywhere inside Ω . In dimension two the singular set is empty. Interior isolation allows accumulation at the boundary and does not imply that the entire singular set is finite. The results here concern interior minimizing maps; boundary regularity, rectifiability, and quantitative stratification are outside their scope. The route to the dimension bound passes through moving-center density upper semicontinuity, concentration of high-density points near planes, and affine covering estimates. The exact final statement is StratificationTheory.stratification . How regularity and interpolation lead to stratification Two complementary inputs support interior stratification for minimizing harmonic maps. Small-energy regularity gives a singular density gap and preliminary Hausdorff nullity. Joint Luckhaus interpolation gives limit minimality and strong compactness. Actual tangent maps, their spines and moving-center density upper semicontinuity lead to plane concentration and Hausdorff covering bounds for strata defined using every actual tangent. In dimension three singularities have no interior accumulation; the separate dimension-two endpoint has no singularities. 03 / STRATIFICATION Regularity becomes geometric control. Interior minimizing maps · strata use every actual tangent Small-energy regularity A proved input from the first project Joint Luckhaus interpolation One connector: traces, energy, distance Singular density gap Regularity ↔ zero density Preliminary Hausdorff nullity Strong local compactness Limit minimality + energy convergence Actual tangent maps Prescribed shrinking scales Strong limits · proved homogeneity Density upper semicontinuity Includes moving centers Uses the prescribed weak limit Linear spines Maximal-density set Translation invariance · dimension bound Concentration near a plane High-density points at small scales Density pieces + affine coverings Hausdorff bounds for universal strata dim ⁡ H S j ( u ) ≤ j , 0 ≤ j ≤ n − 3 Consequently, dim ⁡ H Σ ( u ) ≤ n − 3 n = 2 : Σ ( u ) = ∅ Local energy + small-energy regularity n = 3 : interior isolation No accumulation inside the domain Interior results only · no claim of global finiteness or rectifiability Figure 3. Regularity and Luckhaus interpolation feed different parts of the singular-set argument. The density gap and preliminary Hausdorff nullity are needed alongside tangent-map compactness and covering estimates. The two-dimensional endpoint is proved separately using small-energy regularity. Where mathematical supervision mattered The implementation used Codex with Scott Armstrong’s LeanAutoformalizationSkills . I supplied the mathematical goals and detailed natural-language proofs, separated small energy to Hölder continuity from Hölder continuity to smoothness, and specified the interfaces through which the results would be combined. The workflow involved continued interaction, statement review, dependency planning, and integration. It was not a one-prompt experiment, and it involved no project-specific model training. The important review question was whether the formal assumptions and conclusion still expressed the intended theorem. One intervention concerned dimension. During the Luckhaus construction, the development was heading toward further dimension-specific cases. I redirected it toward a general induction whose state preserved the traces, gradients, energy budgets, and distance bounds needed by the successor step. The resulting coherent recursion supports a dimension-independent construction. Fixed-dimensional components remain, but the general result is obtained by an inductive successor, not by checking a list of dimensions. At the inspected revision, the stratification project contains 712 modules. The project-level import closure of the joint Luckhaus declaration contains 373 modules, including shared infrastructure. These figures indicate the size of the construction and gluing obligations; they are not an exclusive code count for one lemma, or a measure of mathematical difficulty. Can an existential constant become a number? A regularity theorem often finishes with “there exists C .” Inspecting the formal proof can reveal more. In this development, the derivative bootstrap selects constants through Classical.choose and iterates them by recursion. Following the existence proofs exposes explicit arithmetic witnesses. The source report extracts an admissible recurrence of the form M m + 1 = M m + n m + 1 S m ( M m + P m − 1 + Q m − 1 ) . Here S m is a nested-ball Schauder coefficient, and P m − 1 , Q m − 1 bound the differentiated quadratic forcing and its Hölder seminorm. The initial bound M 1 and quantitative coefficient data must already be supplied. The report specifies their dependencies and the arguments of each recurrence. Three levels need to remain distinct. The Lean development proves existential estimates and local witness inequalities. Additional mathematical calculations recombine those witnesses and replace some limit-selected scales by explicit expressions. Finally, scalar scripts numerically evaluate those expressions. The extracted recurrence need not be definitionally equal to the opaque witness chosen by the public theorem. The sphere example illustrates the gap between explicitness and sharpness. For a three-dimensional domain and a unit-sphere target, the report’s deliberately conservative specialization gives log ⁡ 10 ε ∗ ≈ − 2757.66039 , log ⁡ 10 C 2 ≈ 2147.89570. These are approximate evaluations of exact expressions, not interval-certified rounded bounds. The sphere specialization and the extra scalar replacements have not been exported as a new explicit-constant Lean theorem. An abstract compact smooth target also does not supply numerical projection radii or curvature bounds; those geometric inputs must be quantified separately. Verification claims in this post are limited to that dated snapshot. Axiom checks and statement review answer different questions. A proof can pass kernel checking while its declared type is weaker than the intended mathematical claim. Review must therefore inspect the definitions, hypotheses, quantifiers, and shared witnesses, including whether a desired conclusion has accidentally become an assumption. The source report describes a sub-week formalization campaign as my calendar-time account. The retained records do not independently measure all earlier development, mathematical preparation, human hours, or compute usage. It should not be read as a controlled speed or efficiency benchmark. What I would carry into the next project The first lesson is to choose a complete proof with its dependencies in view. A short argument can have a large formal prerequisite cost. The second is to design joint interfaces around the same mathematical objects: the same map, connector, gradient, or subsequence must survive every result that uses it. The third is to make the general induction explicit before repeated low-dimensional work becomes the default. These choices also affect what the resulting library can offer beyond its headline theorem. The quadratic-Poisson upgrade is a reusable analytic component. The joint connector packages geometric construction together with the estimates that make it useful. The constants analysis reveals where numerical information is available and where it still requires additional mathematics. Lean checking does not by itself guarantee readable code, a convenient API, small dependency closures, or fast builds. Those remain practical questions for subsequent use. The value of this formalization is both a checkable account of classical regularity and a clearer specification of the objects and estimates needed to connect it to singular-set geometry.
